transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what's been going on that brought you in today?

I guess the main thing is that I’m just… exhausted. Not just “I had a busy week” tired, but the kind where I sleep and still wake up feeling like I’m carrying something heavy. I’m 46, I work as a manager, and normally I can push through a lot, but lately even getting through a regular workday feels harder than it should. And then coming home and doing something as basic as having dinner or helping with the evening routine just feels like this huge effort.

It’s frustrating because from the outside it probably doesn’t look dramatic. I’m still functioning, mostly. But inside I feel worn down in a way that rest isn’t really fixing, and that’s what made me think I should come in instead of just telling myself to tough it out.
Have you noticed that you’re not enjoying things as much as you used to, even activities that typically make you happy?

Yes… definitely. That’s actually one of the things that makes me feel most unlike myself. I usually really love painting — like, I have my supplies set up, and normally even just looking at the colors or thinking about what I might work on feels calming. But lately they’re just sitting there untouched. I’ll see them and think, “I should do something,” and then I just… don’t. It doesn’t feel worth the effort, or I can’t make myself care enough to start.

And museums too. I used to love wandering through exhibits, taking my time, reading the little descriptions, just getting absorbed in it. Now even the idea of going feels flat. It’s not that I hate it or anything, it’s more like the part of me that used to feel pulled toward those things has gone quiet. It’s upsetting, because those were very much “me” things.
Have you noticed feeling down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, even if it's not severe?

Yes… most days, lately. It’s not always dramatic, like I’m crying all day or something, but I wake up with this heavy, gray feeling. Like the day is already disappointing before it’s even started, if that makes sense.

I’ll open my eyes and there’s this immediate sinking feeling, almost like I’m bracing myself for the day even though nothing has happened yet. And I can still get up and do what I need to do, mostly, so part of me keeps thinking, “Well, maybe it’s not that bad.” But it’s there in the background for a lot of the day. Just this low, flat, discouraged feeling that follows me around.
Have these feelings of low mood, loss of interest, and fatigue been happening most days for at least the past two weeks?

Yes. I’d say it’s definitely been more than two weeks — closer to about a month now, when I really think about it.

It’s a little hard to mark the exact day it started, because it wasn’t like I woke up one morning and everything was suddenly awful. It’s more like there was this shift. I had been in this stretch where I felt unusually energized and driven, like I was pushing forward really hard, and then it kind of swung the other way. Since then, the low mood and the lack of interest and the tiredness have been there most days.

Some days are a little better than others, but it hasn’t really lifted in any lasting way. It’s been persistent enough that I can’t just write it off as a bad week anymore.
Have you noticed a significant loss of energy or feel like even small tasks take a lot of effort lately?

Yes, very much. That’s honestly a big part of what made me feel like I needed to come in. I’m exhausted in a way that doesn’t seem to match what I’m actually doing, if that makes sense. Like, it’s not just “I had a long day and I’m tired.” It’s more like this heavy, whole-body tiredness where even basic things feel like they require this huge push.

I can get through a normal workday, but it feels much harder than it should. I’m a manager, so there are always decisions and emails and people needing things, and lately even keeping up with that feels like I’m dragging myself through it. And then I get home and dinner feels like this whole mountain to climb, even if it’s something simple. I’ll stand there thinking, “This should not be this difficult,” but it is.

And sleep doesn’t really fix it. I keep expecting that if I just rest enough, I’ll wake up and feel more like myself, but I don’t. It’s like the tiredness is still there waiting for me in the morning.
Have you had any days where you felt so down or hopeless that you wondered if life was worth living, or if you had thoughts that you'd be better off dead?

I don’t think so… not in that way. I mean, I’ve felt really discouraged and worn down, and there are moments where I think, “I can’t believe I have to keep getting through another day feeling like this,” but I don’t think I’ve been thinking that I’d be better off dead.

It’s more like I want the heaviness to stop, or I want to feel like myself again. I don’t want to disappear, exactly. I just get tired of pushing through everything. But no, I haven’t had a plan or anything like that, and I don’t think I’ve been wishing I wouldn’t wake up. It’s more… I’m frustrated and sad and exhausted, if that makes sense, but not wanting to die.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight recently, like a decrease in appetite or significant weight loss?

Yes, I think so. I wouldn’t say it’s been dramatic, or at least I haven’t weighed myself and seen some big number change, but I have noticed I’m just not eating the way I normally do.

At work especially, I’ll realize halfway through the afternoon that I never really ate lunch, or I’ll have brought something and just sort of pick at it and then forget about it. It’s not that I’m intentionally skipping meals or trying to diet. Food just doesn’t seem very appealing, or it feels like too much effort to stop and deal with it.

And then with weight… again, I don’t know an exact number, but some of my skirts have been fitting a little looser lately. Not falling off or anything, but enough that I noticed it when I was getting dressed. I remember thinking, “That’s odd,” because I’m definitely not trying to lose weight right now.
Have you found yourself feeling guilty or like you're not good enough for things, even when there's no real reason for it?

Yes… I do. Probably more than I want to admit.

It’s not like I’m sitting there thinking, “I’m a terrible person” all day, but I keep going back over things in my head. Like if I missed something with the kids, or we had some family plan and I just didn’t have it in me to follow through, I’ll replay it later and feel awful. Even if no one is making a big deal about it, I’ll think, “Why couldn’t I just do that? Other people manage to show up for their families.”

And with my husband, if we have a tense conversation or I’m short with him, I’ll keep turning it over afterward, like I’m building a whole case against myself. I start feeling like I’m failing as a wife, like he’s having to deal with this version of me who isn’t very present or warm or helpful.

It happens at work too. I know, rationally, I’m still doing my job, but because I’m not feeling like myself, I keep thinking I’m letting people down there too. Like as a manager I should be more on top of things, more steady, more available. So yes, there’s this constant sense that I’m not doing enough, or I’m disappointing everyone — my family, my husband, people at work. Even when there isn’t one clear thing I can point to that I actually did wrong.
Have you noticed yourself moving more slowly than usual, or on the flip side, feeling restless or fidgety in a way that’s unusual for you?

Yes… I think more on the “slowed down” side than restless. I haven’t noticed myself pacing or fidgeting a lot, but I have noticed — and other people have noticed, which is the embarrassing part — that I’m slower to respond sometimes.

Like in meetings at work, someone will ask me a question that normally I’d answer pretty quickly, and there’s this pause where I feel like my brain is trying to catch up. I know I know the answer, but it takes a second for the thought to form and then another second to get the words out. My staff has kind of gently pointed it out, not in a mean way, but I can tell they’re waiting on me more than usual.

It’s not that I don’t understand what they’re asking. It’s more like everything has a delay on it. And then I get self-conscious because I’m the manager, so I’m supposed to be the person who can respond and make decisions, and instead I’m sitting there with this awkward pause before I can get myself moving verbally.
Have you noticed that your thoughts are slowed down or that you’re moving more slowly than usual, almost like you’re in slow motion?

Yes, that’s exactly how it feels, at least in certain situations. I don’t know if I’d say my whole body is in slow motion all day, but my thinking and my responses definitely feel slower than they used to.

The place I notice it most is in meetings at work. Someone on my staff will ask me something — something I should be able to answer pretty normally, because it’s not like I don’t know the information — and there’s this pause. Like I hear the question, and I understand it, but it takes a few extra seconds for my brain to organize the thought, and then a few more seconds for the words to actually come out.

And I think my staff has noticed too, which makes me feel really self-conscious. They’re not rude about it, but I can tell sometimes they’re waiting for me to answer, and I’m just sitting there trying to get my thoughts moving. It’s embarrassing because I’m used to being quicker than that, especially as the person who’s supposed to be leading the meeting.
Have you been having trouble sleeping, like trouble falling asleep, waking up during the night, or waking up too early in the morning?

Yes. It’s not so much that I can’t fall asleep at all — I usually can get myself into bed at a reasonable time now, and I’ll fall asleep eventually — but I’ve been waking up really early. Like around four or five in the morning.

And once I’m awake, that’s kind of it. My mind just starts going. I’ll be lying there thinking about work, things I need to handle, whether I missed something, conversations I need to have… and then it shifts into my marriage, like replaying things with my husband or worrying about where we are. It’s not even useful thinking. It’s just this loop.

I’ll try to tell myself to go back to sleep because it’s still dark and I don’t need to be up yet, but once those thoughts start, my body is tired but my brain is done sleeping. So I just lie there, sometimes for an hour or more, hoping I’ll drift off again, but most mornings I don’t really get back to sleep.
Have you ever experienced a period of time before this one where you felt down, lost interest in things, or had similar symptoms that lasted for several weeks or more?

Yes… there was a stretch before this that I can pretty clearly remember. The longest one was probably about five months, if I’m thinking of it honestly.

It wasn’t like I was crying every single day or anything dramatic like that, but I felt low most days, and tired in this heavy way that didn’t feel like normal tiredness. I just didn’t feel like myself. It went on long enough that it became hard to tell where “having a bad week” ended and where it was something more persistent.

I remember looking back afterward and thinking, okay, that wasn’t just a mood. That was months of me feeling off — like I was moving through life, doing what I had to do, but not really feeling like me. So yes, I’d say several weeks, definitely. More like months. Five months is the longest one I can clearly point to.

patient.answer:
Yes… there was a stretch before this that I can pretty clearly remember. The longest one was probably about five months, if I’m thinking of it honestly.

It wasn’t like I was crying every single day or anything dramatic like that, but I felt low most days, and tired in this heavy way that didn’t feel like normal tiredness. I just didn’t feel like myself. It went on long enough that it became hard to tell where “having a bad week” ended and where it was something more persistent.

I remember looking back afterward and thinking, okay, that wasn’t just a mood. That was months of me feeling off — like I was moving through life, doing what I had to do, but not really feeling like me. So yes, I’d say several weeks, definitely. More like months. Five months is the longest one I can clearly point to.

inference.note: The patient has a history of a previous depressive episode lasting five months, and the current episode has lasted over a month with persistent low mood, anhedonia, fatigue, slowed psychomotor functioning, early morning awakening, and feelings of guilt and worthlessness. These factors confirm the diagnosis of a recurrent depressive disorder, current episode severe.

opening_question.intent: To establish the patient's reason for seeking psychiatric evaluation
opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what's been going on that brought you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets criteria for a major depressive episode with recurrence and moderate severity. The symptoms have persisted for more than a month, include depressed mood, anhedonia, fatigue, psychomotor slowing, insomnia, guilt, and reduced appetite, with significant functional impairment. There is also a clear history of a prior episode lasting several months, confirming recurrence.
